thread: Follow the swarm from the many lives of butterflies and moths into the extraordinary machinery of insects, then to a museum cabinet full of their relatives. Caterpillars change shape, mouthparts become tools, and tiny bodies unfold into a multitude of designs.

candidates.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America
candidates.why: Species profiles, caterpillars, wing patterns, host plants, and regional sightings offer thousands of starting shapes for a swarm undergoing metamorphosis.

candidates.name: NC State General Entomology
candidates.why: Insect identification pages and bite-sized lessons explore water striders, disguised caterpillars, insect defenses, mouthparts, and the many orders of insects.

candidates.name: Bohart Museum of Entomology
candidates.why: Insect fact sheets, native bees, a cabbage white life cycle, and unusual collections including water bears fill a museum with small, varied creatures.

candidates.name: UC Riverside Entomology Research Museum
candidates.why: Specimen preparation guides, insect spotlights, desert surveys, and collections of blister beetles and tiny parasitic wasps reveal how insects are studied and preserved.

candidates.name: Bumblebee Conservation Trust
candidates.why: Bumblebee species, queens, workers, nests, and pollen baskets offer a colony-sized variation on the insect journey.

candidates.name: Missouri Department of Conservation
candidates.why: Its field guide contains butterflies, moths, beetles, and other invertebrates with life histories and habitats for a swarm exploring a real landscape.

candidates.name: Australian Museum
candidates.why: Animal profiles introduce Australian ants, insects, spiders, and other invertebrates, including colonies and striking adaptations from another continent.

candidates.name: Montana Field Guide
candidates.why: Linked animal groups and species accounts give the swarm beetles, bees, butterflies, and other inhabitants of Montana's habitats to encounter.
